processes.description: Desk leads, mainly Bill Williams, arrange the telephony and computer kit for trading and real-time desks: turret handsets, an extra turret, PCs, headsets, cable moves and a group mobile phone plan. A round starts with a request to IT, the telecoms team or a carrier. The order is logged and assigned to a deployment technician, who reports when installation is complete. Others check whether ordered or invoiced items arrived, collect turret IDs, set limits on the calling plan and cancel services no longer needed.
steps: A desk lead identifies equipment a desk or person needs, such as handsets, a turret, a PC, a headset or a phone plan.
The request goes to IT, the telecoms team or the carrier, by email or by phoning in the order.
The order is logged and assigned to a deployment technician, who confirms the work has started.
The technician installs the equipment or moves cabling and sends a completion notice.
The requester confirms that ordered items arrived and matches vendor invoices to what was received.
For phone plans, limits are set, members are told their usage, and services nobody uses are cancelled.

stalls.summary: A request for a phone for a new person sat with the outside carrier, and the desk lead had to chase for news.
Nothing confirms receipt automatically: after a vendor invoice for supplies turned up, a requester had to be asked to check whether the items had actually arrived.

automation.approach: A shared equipment request tracker with one row per request: desk, person, item, vendor or carrier, order reference, assigned technician, status, receipt confirmed and invoice matched. Completion notices from the deployment system and vendor invoices update the row, and rows still open after their expected date are listed for follow-up. The same sheet keeps turret IDs and phone plan members, so those lists are not rebuilt each time someone asks.
automation.rationale: Rounds are small orders spread across IT, telecoms, a carrier and vendors. The work that repeats is keeping track of what was ordered, whether it arrived, which invoice it matches, and collecting turret IDs and plan details again. One tracking layout covers all of that. Placing orders and installing equipment stay manual.

work_estimate.rationale: The hands-on work in a round is phoning in or keying an order, a technician installing a PC or moving cable, checking receipt against an invoice, or compiling turret IDs or plan usage. Most rounds show one such small task, so the middle figure is 15 minutes. A simple order or cancellation takes 5 minutes, and an install or cable move up to 60. A tracker could take over the tracking, receipt matching and lists. Installs and carrier calls stay manual.

processes.description: Logistics and desk leads decide who schedules which pipelines, pooling points, meters, industrial accounts and counterparties, and announce the changes to the group. A round starts with a reorganisation, a new point or meter, cross-training or a change of role. A lead such as Pat Clynes sends out the new assignments, the person taking over confirms, and the previous owner hands over the accounts. Follow-ups flag items left unassigned, send error-report items to the right person, and ask someone to pick up work such as pipeline rates from another team.
steps: A lead decides a change in coverage after a reorganisation, a new meter or point, cross-training or a change of role.
The lead announces who will handle which pipelines, meters, books or counterparties.
The incoming person confirms taking over, and the outgoing owner hands over the accounts and how to run them.
Each rep updates pathing and records in the scheduling system for the meters in their assigned zones.
Colleagues flag items that are unassigned or with the wrong person and ask who owns them.
The lead settles the open items and confirms the arrangement with everyone involved.

stalls.summary: Items fall through the announced assignments: one business unit is noticed to have no owner, and a later message asks who owns an item for the month and marks it unresolved.
A handover leaves the new owner without the know-how: a person told to pick up another team's off-system pipeline rates says she has no idea how and asks for time to talk it through.
The handover of the industrial accounts drags on: the outgoing scheduler says the new owner would not have known how to handle one account, and only later leaves the accounts to him.
A planned change waits on one person: the lead confirms the change is still on but has not yet spoken to one trader.
Items on the error report sit with someone other than their owner until the owner asks for them to be referred to her.

contradictions.summary: The mail disagrees about who owns the industrial accounts. One message says they should be fully transferred to Robert, and Robert says he has taken over all of them. Yet the outgoing scheduler is still handling one account because Robert would not have known how.
A message states that each logistics rep paths all meters in their assigned zones, yet in the same round a business unit turns out to have no owner.

automation.approach: A single maintained coverage roster listing every pipeline, pooling point, meter, book and counterparty with its primary and backup owner and the date each assignment takes effect. A change is entered once and the announcement is produced from the roster. A check lists entries with no owner, and error-report items held by someone other than the listed owner. A short handover checklist goes with each reassignment.
automation.rationale: The stalls come from items left out of announcements and from owners changing without the knowledge moving with them. A roster that flags items with no owner catches the gaps before the month starts, and producing announcements from it removes the retyping. Deciding who covers what and training the successor remain work for people.

work_estimate.rationale: The hands-on work in a round is deciding the new split of pipelines and meters, writing up the assignment list, updating meter pathing and assignments in the scheduling system, and briefing the successor on the accounts. Most rounds are a short reassignment list, so the middle figure is 25 minutes. A single meter assignment takes 10, and a handover of several accounts with training up to 60. A roster could produce the lists and catch unassigned items. The decisions and the training stay manual.

processes.description: Managers and staff ask HR or payroll to change employee records. Requests include moving employees to a different operating company, stopping payroll deductions such as United Way contributions from a stated date, adding staff missing from the HR system, arranging an exit interview, and clarifying a departing employee's separation entitlements. In a round, someone sends a request to HR, HR looks up or changes the record, and HR confirms back to the requester, who may pass the answer on to the employee.
steps: A manager or employee asks HR or payroll to change a record, a deduction or an entitlement.
HR looks up the employee in the HR system and checks what is recorded.
HR makes the change, adds the missing person, or works out the entitlement in question.
HR confirms the outcome to the requester.
The requester passes the answer on to the employee or arranges the next step, such as an exit interview.

stalls.summary: A manager answering a departing employee's request for clarification had to wait for HR and asked to be told as soon as there was an answer.
One new employee was in the system and another was not, so the missing record had to be set up before the request could go ahead.

automation.approach: A standard HR change request form that records the employee, the type of change (operating company, supervisor, deduction or separation), the date it takes effect and the approver. The form goes to the HR contact and shows the requester its status. Employees could stop deductions themselves, and a new-starter check could compare the HR system with the team roster to flag anyone missing.
automation.rationale: The rounds are short requests, slowed by missing details and by waiting for a reply. A form with the fields HR needs, and a status the requester can see, cuts the back-and-forth. Separation entitlements and exits still need HR's judgement.

work_estimate.rationale: The hands-on work is HR looking up the employee and entering the record or deduction change, and for departures working out entitlements and holding the exit interview. Most rounds are a single record change, so the middle figure is 10 minutes. Stopping a deduction takes 5 minutes, and checking separation terms up to 30. A form and employee self-service could take over the routine changes. Entitlements and exits stay with HR.
